title: China’s AI Chip Ambitions Hit a Memory Wall
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Chinese artificial-intelligence chipmakers are raising prices as a global shortage of high-bandwidth memory increases production costs and complicates Beijing’s drive to replace Nvidia hardware with domestic alternatives.

Huawei has reportedly lifted the indicated price of its upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator card to more than 250,000 yuan, or roughly $37,255. Depending on contract terms, that represents a 20% to 50% increase from quotations issued two months earlier. Cambricon has raised indicative pricing for its next-generation 690 chip by 20% to 30%, while smaller competitors MetaX and Iluvatar CoreX have made similar adjustments.

The pressure comes from HBM, the vertically stacked memory placed close to AI processors to deliver the enormous bandwidth required for training and inference. Memory is a substantial part of an accelerator card’s bill of materials. When HBM costs rise, chip vendors have limited room to absorb the increase without damaging margins.

Supply is especially difficult in China. Advanced HBM production is concentrated among SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics and Micron. US export controls tightened in December 2024, restricting China’s access to certain advanced HBM products. Chinese companies have consequently turned to expensive grey-market supplies, where memory can cost several times more than it does for buyers elsewhere.

Older hardware is also becoming more expensive. Huawei’s Ascend 950PR has risen from about 60,000 yuan early this year to more than 80,000 yuan, while the Ascend 910C has increased from roughly 90,000 yuan to above 110,000 yuan.

The shortage reveals an important weakness in semiconductor self-sufficiency strategies: producing the compute die is only part of the challenge. AI accelerators also depend on advanced memory, packaging, interconnects and software. Until domestic HBM capacity improves, Chinese suppliers may gain market share from Nvidia restrictions while still facing higher costs, constrained volumes and slower infrastructure deployment.

Source: Reuters
